title: The debugger can lose the start race to the plugin's automatic restart
body:
Found by the box that landed #4.

## What happens
Running **se: debug this workspace's daemon** in VS Code stops the workspace's daemon, then starts `se serve` under Delve. If a session in that workspace is switched on, the plugin sees the daemon gone and starts a new one. When that happens before the debugged `se serve` starts, the debugged one fails with "a daemon already runs", and the person's breakpoints never get an event.

## What should happen
Starting the daemon under the debugger takes the workspace over reliably, every time. One possible approach is for the debugged `se serve` to ask a running daemon to step down instead of refusing. Pick whatever is simplest and robust, and cover it with a test.

title: work skill: a box takes the next se issue and lands it
body:
Blocked by: #5

## Why
Boxes are cloud sessions that work unattended. Each one is started with the prompt `run the work skill`. The skill is the whole procedure, so one prompt runs any box, and a routine can start them on a schedule or on demand.

## The task
Write `.claude/skills/work/SKILL.md` (and link it from the README). The procedure:
1. Make sure the checkout is the current `origin/main`, then run `se issue take`. If nothing is ready, say so in one line and end.
2. Rename this session to `SE #<n> · <issue title>` (with `set_session_title`, if available), so the session list, the issue and the PR share one number.
3. Do the issue's work, following CLAUDE.md. Decide every step yourself; nobody watches live.
4. Run `sh ./tests/check.sh` until it passes.
5. Push, open one PR against main whose body says `Fixes #<n>`, and turn on auto-merge with SQUASH.
6. Subscribe to the PR's activity and drive it to green: a red CI run is yours to fix on the same branch.
7. If the work turns up something that belongs in a separate change, open a new issue labelled `se` for it (with a `Blocked by:` line where it waits on something) rather than widening the PR.
8. When the PR has merged, or when you are stuck on a decision only the owner can make, send one message to the session that started you, if it is a session and `send_message` is available. End with one line giving the issue, the PR link and the outcome.

## Proving it
Start one box with `run the work skill` once the skill is on main. It should take the lowest-numbered ready `se` issue and land it.

title: se issue next / se issue take: pick and claim the next ready se issue
body:
## Why
SE's work items are GitHub issues. A box must find the next issue it may work on and claim it so no other box takes it. The choice has to be deterministic, so it lives in Go (`se`), not in a prompt.

## The rules (decided with the owner; write them into `docs/issues.md`, the one place they live, and link it from the README)
- **Fleet work**: an open issue carrying the label `se`. Other issues are not the fleet's.
- **Blockers**: an issue waits while any of its blockers is open. Blockers are GitHub's native "blocked by" links, plus any line in the body of the form `Blocked by: #12, #14`. Agents use the body line because their GitHub tools cannot write native links. Honour both.
- **Claimed**: an issue whose branch `issue-<n>` exists on origin is claimed. A box claims an issue by pushing that branch from the current `origin/main`. A push is atomic, so if two boxes race, the second push fails and that box moves to the next issue.
- **Order**: the lowest issue number among the ready ones.
- **Done**: the PR's body says `Fixes #n`, so GitHub closes the issue when the PR merges, and the issues it blocked become ready.

## The task
1. `se issue next` prints the next ready issue (number, title, body), or says that none is ready. It exits 0 either way and offers `--json`.
2. `se issue take [n]` claims the next ready issue, or issue `n`: it creates the branch `issue-<n>` from `origin/main`, pushes it and checks it out. If the push is refused because the branch exists, it moves to the next ready issue. It prints what it took, or that nothing is ready.
3. Both read GitHub through the `gh` CLI (`gh api`), which owns authentication. On cloud boxes `gh` already reaches the API. Add `gh` to `RUNME.sh`'s dependencies: if it is missing, name how to install it; if `gh auth status` fails, ask the person to run `gh auth login`.
4. Register both as commands in the existing command registry (`cmd/se/commands.go`, one file per command). `next` may also be offered in a session as `/se issue next`. If the registry has no notion of sub-words yet, make `issue` take a sub-word.
5. Tests: the selection logic (labels, both kinds of blockers, claimed branches, ordering, nothing ready) runs against recorded `gh` answers, so CI needs no network. The race (a second push refused) is tested against a local bare repository.

## Proving it
`sh ./tests/check.sh` passes. On a cloud box, `se issue next` against mb-89/SE names a real open `se` issue.
